**Given:** The finite chain $\Sigma$, the smooth family $\alpha_p$, and the
stated joint smoothness of its pullback coefficients.

[F1] A smooth singular chain is a finite real linear combination of smooth
singular simplices. [[def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes]]

[F2] The integral over a smooth three-simplex is the Jordan Riemann integral
of its pullback coefficient on the standard simplex domain
$T_3=\{z\in\mathbb R^3:z_i\ge0,\ z_1+z_2+z_3\le1\}$.
[[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]

[F3] Integration over a bounded Jordan set is defined by extending the
integrand by zero to a bounded containing rectangle and integrating there.
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]

[F4] On a rectangle, the Darboux integral is the common value of the
supremum of lower grid sums and infimum of upper grid sums; common refinements
preserve the integral criterion. [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]

[F5] A rectangle has finite volume, and cutting one coordinate interval
preserves total volume. [[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]

[F6] A closed bounded subset of Euclidean space is compact.
[[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F7] A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly
continuous. [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]

[F8] For a continuously differentiable function on a closed interval, the
integral of its derivative is the endpoint increment.
[[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]



**Given:** As in [F1]–[F8].

1.1 First consider integration on one simplex, using the zero extension in [F3] to a bounded nondegenerate rectangle $Q$. The Darboux definitions [F4] give linearity: for integrable $u,w$, choose grid partitions whose upper-minus lower sums for each are arbitrarily small, take a common refinement, and use $\inf(u+w)\ge\inf u+\inf w$ and $\sup(u+w)\le\sup u+\sup w$ on each cell. The upper-minus-lower gap for $u+w$ is therefore bounded by the sum of the chosen gaps, so $u+w$ is integrable. Its lower and upper integrals are squeezed between the sums of the lower integrals of $u,w$ and the sums of their upper integrals; letting the gaps tend to zero gives $\int_Q(u+w)=\int_Qu+\int_Qw$. For a scalar $c>0$, upper and lower sums scale by $c$; for $c<0$ they exchange after scaling, giving $\int_Q(cu)=c\int_Qu$, and $c=0$ gives zero. Also, if $|u|\le\varepsilon$ on $Q$, each lower sum is at least $-\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ and each upper sum at most $\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$, since cell volumes add to $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ by [F5]. Thus $|\int_\sigma u|\le\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ for an integrable function on the simplex bounded by $\varepsilon$. [F3, F4, F5]

2.1 Fix a parameter chart and a point $p$. For one simplex $\sigma$ write $\sigma^*\alpha_p=f(p,z)\,dz_1\wedge dz_2\wedge dz_3$ on $T_3$. Choose a closed parameter rectangle $R$ around $p$ inside the chart. The displayed inequalities defining $T_3$ make it closed and bounded, hence compact by [F6]; [F2] identifies it as the integration domain. The product $R\times T_3$ is a closed bounded Euclidean set, hence compact by [F6], so $\partial_a f$ is uniformly continuous there by [F7]. For a small nonzero increment $h$ in coordinate $p^a$, [F8] gives $$\frac{f(p+he_a,z)-f(p,z)}{h}-\partial_af(p,z) =\frac1h\int_0^h\bigl(\partial_af(p+se_a,z)-\partial_af(p,z)\bigr)\,ds.$$ Uniform continuity makes the right side tend uniformly to zero on $T_3$ as $h\to0$. By step 1.1, the integral of this error tends to zero. Linearity therefore gives $$\partial_a\int_\sigma f(p,z)\,dz=\int_\sigma\partial_af(p,z)\,dz.$$ Applying the same argument to every parameter derivative of $f$ proves that all parameter partial derivatives of the simplex integral exist and are integrals of the corresponding derivatives. They are continuous: on a compact parameter rectangle, uniform continuity of each next derivative and step 1.1 bound the change in its integral by the uniform coefficient change times $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$. Hence this simplex integral is smooth. [F2, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F1], $\Sigma$ is a finite linear combination of such simplices. Linearity from step 1.1 makes $I$ the corresponding finite linear combination of their smooth integrals and gives the asserted derivative formula for every parameter coordinate. Linearity in the tangent vector then gives the formula for every $v\in T_pP$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎



The chain is fixed and finite, and the parameter manifold is finite
dimensional. No infinite-chain convergence or infinite-dimensional field
space structure is part of the lemma.

**Given:** Countable Choice, Dependent Choice, the fixed finite-slab comparison context, one coefficient family and gauge, the stated solution and source regularity, common compact state ranges, the separate $H^s$ and time-derivative bounds $R_z,R_t$, and the positive lower bound for $A^0$.

[A1] The geometric application assumes the countable- and dependent-choice hypotheses used by the local development construction ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).

[F1] A fixed-gauge comparison context uses the same coefficient family and coordinate grid on the same torus; states belong to $L^\infty(J;H^s)\cap C^0(J;H^{s-1})$, with separate uniform bounds $R_z$ and $R_t$ on the state and its time derivative, and $A^0$ has the stated uniform positive lower bound ([[def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology]]).

[F2] For the homogeneous periodic system, bounded $H^s$ solutions with values in a compact coefficient set are unique and satisfy an $H^{s-1}$ continuous-dependence estimate on each fixed compact time interval ([[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-uniqueness-stability]]).

[F3] Smooth coefficients on compact value sets have $H^{s-1}$ composition-difference and commutator bounds; the difference bound is proportional to the $H^{s-1}$ norm of the state difference, and spatial/time commutators have the orders stated in the supplier ([[lem-gr-smooth-composition-and-commutator-estimates]]).

[F4] A continuous positive-definite symmetric matrix family on a compact parameter set has uniform bounds $aI\le A^0\le bI$ for some $0<a\le b<\infty$ ([[lem-gr-positive-definite-symmetric-matrix-bounds]]).

[F5] For a compact admissible state set and bounded $H^s$ data, the periodic existence theorem gives a common positive local time and a uniform $H^s$ solution bound ([[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-existence]]).

[F6] For smooth data, the higher-order energy refinement bounds the $H^s$ norm on a finite interval from a bound on the lower $H^{s-1}$ norm; the proof gives $|E_s'|\le C_\rho(1+E_s)$ and the continuation argument uses the fixed local existence time ([[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-smooth-persistence]]).

[F7] On $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $H^{s-1}\subset C^0$ continuously for $s\ge5$ ([[lem-gr-periodic-sobolev-embedding]]).

[F8] For one fixed Einstein-matter model, complete constrained data satisfying the local reduction, compatibility, conservation and positivity hypotheses yield a local full development and data-fixing geometric uniqueness; this does not assert a uniform noncompact collar or global-in-time existence ([[thm-gr-local-geometric-development]]).

[F13] For a smooth harmonic-gauge reduced Einstein-matter solution with covariantly conserved stress, if the gauge residual vanishes and the normal Einstein constraints hold on a spacelike slice, then the residual vanishes and the full Einstein equations hold on a neighborhood of that slice ([[thm-gr-harmonic-constraint-propagation]]).

[F9] The strict-fluid local result requires $\epsilon+p>0$ and $0<p'(\epsilon)<1$, excluding shocks, vacuum boundaries and vanishing sound speed; the dust local result does not assert continuation past flow crossings ([[thm-gr-barotropic-fluid-local-evolution]], [[thm-gr-dust-local-evolution]]).

[F10] Fourier projections are self-adjoint, commute with derivatives, contract in each $H^q$, and have a uniform one-order tail bound ([[lem-gr-galerkin-projection-properties]]).

[F11] The maximal-development theorem asserts existence and maximality in the smooth globally hyperbolic class, with uniqueness up to a unique data-fixing isometry; its Statement gives no quantitative stability estimate uniform over arbitrarily long slabs ([[thm-gr-smooth-maximal-globally-hyperbolic-development]]).

[F12] The full initial constraints for $(h,K_{\rm ext},d)$ are the Hamiltonian and momentum equations with the stress tensor $T_0$ computed from the complete branch data, in the convention $K_{\rm ext}(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ ([[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]).

**Proof technique:** direct energy estimate and finite restart.



1.1 Let $r=s-1$. By [F1] and compactness of $J\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times K_2$, all coefficient derivatives needed below are bounded and $A^0(u)$ is uniformly symmetric positive definite; [F4] gives equivalent weighted and unweighted $H^r$ norms. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 Put $w=u-v$ and $F=F_u-F_v$. Subtracting the two equations and adding and subtracting each coefficient evaluated at $u$ gives $A^0(u)\partial_tw+\sum_iA^i(u)\partial_iw=F+Q$, where $Q=-(A^0(u)-A^0(v))\partial_tv-\sum_i(A^i(u)-A^i(v))\partial_iv-B(u)+B(v)$. This is an identity: the coefficient-difference terms multiplying derivatives of $v$ and the difference of the zero-order terms are exactly the residual after the common principal operator is applied to $w$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.3 Fix a smooth reference solution $\bar u$ with state range in $K_0$. Compactness gives a positive distance $d$ from its range to the complement of $\operatorname{int}K_1$. Put $\rho:=1+\|\bar u\|_{C(J;H^r)}$ and take initial data in an $H^s$ ball of radius at most $1$ about $\bar u(0)$, so their $H^s$ norms have a common bound $R_0:=1+\|\bar u(0)\|_{H^s}$. On any solution interval where $\|u-\bar u\|_{C(H^r)}<1$, the lower norm is at most $\rho$. The high-order energy differential inequality in [F6], integrated from the initial slice and using this lower bound, gives one finite bound $M=M(R_0,\rho,T)$ for $\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$ throughout every such interval of existence; it continues to hold across uniqueness-glued restarts because the solution and its energy agree at each join. Choose $R_*>M$. Let $K_{\rm mid}$ be the closed state-space tube of radius $d/3$ about the reference range; it is compact and contained in $\operatorname{int}K_1$. Since the coefficient time interval is open and contains compact $J$, choose $\tau_0>0$ so every translate centered at $t_0\in J$ is defined on $[-\tau_0,\tau_0]$. On the resulting compact time-state set, all coefficient bounds used in the Galerkin proof of [F5] are uniform and $A^0\ge aI$. Apply that proof to each translated family $A^\mu(t_0+\sigma,x,z),B(t_0+\sigma,x,z)$ with input set $K_{\rm mid}$, output set $K_1$ and norm radius $R_*$. The common coefficient bounds, state margin and radius give one local time $\tau_*>0$, decreased if necessary so $\tau_*\le\tau_0$, and one solution bound $M_{\rm loc}$ independent of $t_0$. Smooth persistence [F6] gives smooth local solutions for the smooth restart data. [given, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 The composition-difference estimates in [F3], the state bound $\|v\|_{L^\infty H^s}\le R_z$, and the time-derivative bound $\|\partial_tv\|_{L^\infty H^r}\le R_t$ from [F1] imply $\|Q(t)\|_{H^r}\le C\|w(t)\|_{H^r}$. Solving the displayed difference equation for $\partial_tw$ with $(A^0(u))^{-1}$, whose operator norm is at most $a^{-1}$ by [F4], and using multiplier bounds at order $r-1$ from [F3] gives $\|\partial_tw(t)\|_{H^{r-1}}\le C(\|w(t)\|_{H^r}+\|F(t)\|_{H^{r-1}})$; here $\|\partial_iw\|_{H^{r-1}}\le\|w\|_{H^r}$. [step 1.2, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 Define $E(t)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}(D^\alpha w)^{\mathsf T}A^0(t,x,u)D^\alpha w\,dx$. Put $a=A^0(t,x,u)$, $a_i=A^i(t,x,u)$, $y_\alpha=D^\alpha w$, and $h=\partial_tw$. For $E_N:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int(P_Ny_\alpha)^{\mathsf T}a(P_Ny_\alpha)$, the finite Fourier sums $P_Nw$ are $C^1$ in time by classical regularity, and differentiation gives $E_N'=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}(2\langle P_ND^\alpha h,aP_Ny_\alpha\rangle+\langle P_Ny_\alpha,\partial_ta\,P_Ny_\alpha\rangle)$. The one-order tail estimate [F10] gives $P_Ny_\alpha\to y_\alpha$ uniformly in $L^2$, since $w$ is bounded in $H^{r+1}$. Self-adjointness changes the first pairing to $\langle D^\alpha h,P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)\rangle$. The product $ay_\alpha$ is uniformly bounded in $H^1$ by the Leibniz rule and uniform $C^1$ bound on $a$, so $\|P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)-ay_\alpha\|_2\le\|a\|_\infty\|P_Ny_\alpha-y_\alpha\|_2+\|(P_N-I)(ay_\alpha)\|_2\to0$ uniformly on $J$. Because $D^\alpha h$ is uniformly bounded in $L^2$, the first pairings converge in $L^1(J)$; the quadratic pairings converge uniformly since $\partial_ta$ is bounded. Thus $E_N\to E$ uniformly and $E_N'\to\mathcal G$ in $L^1$, where $\mathcal G=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}(2\langle D^\alpha h,ay_\alpha\rangle+\langle y_\alpha,\partial_ta\,y_\alpha\rangle)$. Passing to the limit in $E_N(t)-E_N(t')=\int_{t'}^tE_N'$ shows $E$ is absolutely continuous and $E'=\mathcal G$ almost everywhere. Differentiating the difference equation in space is an $L^2$ identity almost everywhere because $w\in L^\infty H^{r+1}$, $h\in L^\infty H^r$, and $F+Q\in L^\infty(J;H^r)$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1; periodicity gives no boundary term. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F3, F10, algebra]

4.1 The derivatives of $A^\mu(t,x,u)$ are bounded on the fixed compact coefficient set. The $Q$ term is bounded by [step 2.1]; the commutator terms by [F3] and the $H^{r-1}$ bound on $\partial_tw$ from that step; and the forcing pairing $\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\langle D^\alpha w,D^\alpha F\rangle$ by $\|w\|_{H^r}\|F\|_{H^r}$. Absorbing the quadratic lower-order terms with $2xy\le x^2+y^2$ while retaining the forcing pairing in mixed form, and using [F4] for energy equivalence, gives $E'(t)\le C E(t)+C\sqrt{E(t)}\|F(t)\|_{H^r}$ and $a\|w(t)\|_{H^r}^2\le E(t)\le b\|w(t)\|_{H^r}^2$ almost everywhere. The convergence established in step 3.1 justifies all time-derivative and commutator pairings. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F4, F10, algebra]

5.1 For $\varepsilon>0$, set $Y_\varepsilon=(E+\varepsilon)^{1/2}$. Step 4.1 gives $Y_\varepsilon'\le (C/2)Y_\varepsilon+(C/2)\|F\|_{H^r}$, hence integration yields $Y_\varepsilon(t)\le e^{Ct/2}Y_\varepsilon(0)+(C/2)\int_0^t e^{C(t-r')/2}\|F(r')\|_{H^r}\,dr'$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using the energy equivalence of step 4.1 gives the stated estimate after enlarging $C$ to absorb $\sqrt{b/a}$ and $C/2$. When $F=0$, it is the homogeneous estimate. [step 4.1, F4, algebra]

6.1 Fix the comparison constant in step 5.1 using the bounds $R_*$ and the corresponding time-derivative bound supplied by the unforced equation, [F3] and [F4]. Choose the initial $H^s$ radius so small that this estimate keeps $\|u-\bar u\|_{C(J;H^r)}<\min\{1,d/(4C_{\rm emb})\}$, where $C_{\rm emb}$ is the embedding constant from [F7]. On every partial interval of existence, a first exit from either bootstrap bound is impossible: the strict estimate persists there, the state range lies in $K_{\rm mid}$, and step 1.3 bounds the $H^s$ norm strictly below $R_*$. If a constructed interval ends before $T$, its endpoint data therefore lie in $K_{\rm mid}$ with $H^s$ norm below $R_*$. Step 1.3 supplies a restarted solution on a time interval centered there, with $H^s$ norm at most $M_{\rm loc}$; the previous and restarted solutions overlap to the left of the restart time. Uniqueness [F2], applied with the common bound $\max\{R_*,M_{\rm loc}\}$, identifies them on that overlap. The same bootstrap bounds then continue on the restarted interval. Since $\tau_*>0$ is independent of the restart point, finitely many such restarts cover $J$. This proves the claimed neighborhood. [step 5.1, step 1.3, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

7.1 For the fixed harmonic-gauge reduction in the geometric clause, let $H$ be its gauge residual and $E$ its Einstein residual. Define $P\subseteq[0,T]$ to consist of times at which $H=0$ and the normal Einstein constraints vanish on the whole slice $\{t\}\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. The given initial gauge condition and constraints put $0$ in $P$. At any $t_0\in P$, the reduced matter solution has conserved stress by the stated fixed-model hypotheses, so [F13] gives an open neighborhood of that entire slice on which $H=0$ and $E=0$. The torus slice is compact, hence this neighborhood contains all slices with $|t-t_0|<\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$; thus $P$ is relatively open. If $t_n\in P$ converges to $t_0$, smoothness of the reduced metric, matter fields and their residuals makes $H=0$ and the normal constraint residuals zero at $t_0$, so $P$ is closed. At an endpoint use [F5] to extend the smooth reduced solution a short distance, and [F2] to identify it with the original solution on the overlap; this makes the same open-set argument valid there. Since $[0,T]$ is connected, $P=[0,T]$. The neighborhoods from [F13] therefore cover the slab, proving the original Einstein-matter equations throughout it. [given, step 6.1, A1, F2, F5, F8, F12, F13, algebra]

8.1 The constant and the number of restarts depend on the chosen finite $T$ and the fixed compact state margin. Neither the estimate nor the restart argument is uniform as $T\to\infty$; [F11] is only an existence/maximality and isometry-uniqueness statement. The strict-fluid and dust qualifications in [F9] remain active: shocks or vacuum boundaries and dust flow crossings lie outside the corresponding local branch. [step 6.1, F9, F11, algebra] ∎



For the SI interpretation, the time coordinate is the length coordinate $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ in metres and the torus coordinates are dimensionless angles. Metric components therefore carry the coordinate-dependent units $[g_{00}]=1$, $[g_{0i}]=\mathrm m$, and $[g_{ij}]=\mathrm m^2$; the state components are divided by fixed unit scales before their numerical Sobolev norms are formed, as specified in [[def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology]]. This item proves an estimate for the mathematical coefficient fields in that fixed convention and makes no empirical assertion.

**Given:** A positive integer $n$, a finite partition of $[0,1]$, one continuous matrix coefficient on each closed subinterval, and the initial matrix $I_n$.

[F1] [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]: a continuous matrix coefficient on a compact interval gives a unique global solution to the linear matrix initial-value problem.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply [F1] on $[t_0,t_1]$ with initial matrix $I_n$ to obtain the unique $C^1$ solution on the first interval. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 For each $j=2,\ldots,m$, apply [F1] on $[t_{j-1},t_j]$ with initial value equal to the terminal value already constructed at $t_{j-1}$. Adjacent solutions agree at their shared endpoint by construction, so the finite family pastes to a continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution on $[0,1]$. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Any other such function has initial value $I_n$ on the first interval, so it agrees there by [F1]. If it agrees through $t_{j-1}$, then it has the same initial value as the constructed solution on the $j$th interval, so [F1] makes them agree there. Induction through the finite partition proves uniqueness on all of $[0,1]$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, induction] ∎

**Given:** A smooth manifold $M$, an open set $U\subseteq M$, and the path and thin-homotopy data of Definition [[def-gr-fx-thin-paths]].

[F1] [[def-gr-fx-thin-paths]]: paths have finite smooth subdivisions; a thin homotopy has fixed endpoints and rank at most one on each smooth curvilinear triangle.

[F2] [[def-equivalence-relation]]: an equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; its quotient consists of its equivalence classes.

[F3] [[def-category]]: category composition is associative and has left and right identities; morphisms retain their domain and codomain.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The relation is reflexive because $H(s,t)=\gamma(t)$ has rank at most one and fixed endpoints. It is symmetric by replacing $s$ with $1-s$. If $H_0$ joins $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_1$ and $H_1$ joins $\gamma_1$ to $\gamma_2$, paste $H_0(2s,t)$ on $0\le s\le\tfrac12$ to $H_1(2s-1,t)$ on $\tfrac12\le s\le1$; their common boundary is the same path $\gamma_1$, so the paste is continuous and piecewise smooth on a finite triangulation, fixes both path endpoints, and has rank at most one on each triangle. Thus the relation is transitive. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 If $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$ and $\delta_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1$ with matching endpoints, paste their homotopies on the first and second halves of the path parameter. The shared endpoint is fixed throughout each homotopy, so the paste is continuous and piecewise smooth; on each piece its differential has image contained in the image of the corresponding homotopy differential, hence rank at most one. Therefore $\delta_0*\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1*\gamma_1$, and composition of classes is well-defined. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $\Gamma$ be the path obtained by placing the three given paths, in order, on the three consecutive thirds of $[0,1]$. Each parenthesized concatenation is $\Gamma\circ\phi_j$ for an increasing piecewise-linear homeomorphism $\phi_j:[0,1]\to[0,1]$; on each affine piece, both $\phi_j$ and $\Gamma$ are smooth. The homotopy $H(s,t)=\Gamma((1-s)\phi_0(t)+s\phi_1(t))$ is fixed at its endpoints. Subdivide the square along the finitely many straight break lines of the two piecewise-linear maps and triangulate the resulting polygons. On each triangle, the argument of $\Gamma$ stays in one smooth path piece, so $H$ is smooth there and its two differential columns are scalar multiples of the single vector $\Gamma'$. Its rank is at most one. Thus the two parenthesizations are thin-homotopic. The same construction between the identity parameter and the parameter map for a path with an inserted constant segment proves both identity laws. [given, F1, F3, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 Put $\lambda(t)=2t$ for $0\le t\le\tfrac12$ and $\lambda(t)=2(1-t)$ for $\tfrac12\le t\le1$. Then $t\mapsto\gamma(\lambda(t))$ traverses $\gamma$ and then its reverse. The map $H(s,t)=\gamma((1-s)\lambda(t))$ joins this path to the constant path at $\gamma(0)$ with both endpoints fixed. After triangulating along $t=\tfrac12$, it is smooth on each piece and its differential has rank at most one because both derivatives are scalar multiples of $\dot\gamma$. Reversing $\gamma$ gives the corresponding contraction of the reverse-then-forward path at $\gamma(1)$. Hence $[\bar\gamma]$ is a two-sided inverse of $[\gamma]$. [given, F1, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The tagged morphism set has well-defined domain and codomain by construction; step 2.1 makes composition independent of representatives, step 3.1 gives associativity, and step 3.2 gives the inverse axiom. Steps 3.1 and 3.2 also provide the two identity laws stated in [F3]. Thus the data form a category in which every morphism is invertible, which is the asserted groupoid. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

**Given:** A smooth matrix connection $\omega$ on $U$, a finite curvilinear-triangle subdivision of a fixed-endpoint thin homotopy $H$, and the path ODE of Definition [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]].

[F1] [[def-gr-fx-thin-paths]]: a thin homotopy is piecewise smooth on finitely many curvilinear triangles, fixes the two path endpoints, and has differential rank at most one on every triangle.

[F2] [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]]: along each smooth path segment, transport is the unique solution of $U'=-\omega(\dot\gamma)U$, with later transport multiplying on the left.

[F3] [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]: $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$ is the curvature matrix two-form, and a Lorentz connection satisfies $\omega^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta\omega=0$.

[F4] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: solutions of a smooth parameter-dependent finite-dimensional ODE depend smoothly on the parameter on a common compact interval.

[F5] [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]: for a continuous matrix coefficient and arbitrary initial matrix, the linear matrix ODE has a unique solution on the given compact interval.

[F6] [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]: the fundamental group consists of based loops modulo endpoint-fixed path homotopy.

[F7] [[thm-qftx-cw-fundamental-group-presentation]]: a finite connected CW complex has the presentation with non-tree 1-cells as generators and 2-cell attaching loops as relators.

[F8] [[def-group-presentation]]: a presentation $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ is the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the normal closure of $R$.

[F9] [[prop-normal-closure-is-products-of-conjugates]]: the normal closure of a set is the set of finite products of conjugates of its elements and their inverses.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On one closed curvilinear triangle $\Delta$ of the subdivision, pull the connection back by the smooth restriction of $H$ and write its two coefficient matrices as $A_s=\omega(H_s)$ and $A_t=\omega(H_t)$. For a smooth family of paths inside $\Delta$, let $U_t=-A_tU$, $U(s,0)=I$, and put $K=U_s+A_sU$. Smooth dependence in [F4] permits this differentiation, and [F5] gives uniqueness for the linear equation satisfied by $K$. The product rule gives $K_t+A_tK=-(\partial_sA_t-\partial_tA_s+[A_s,A_t])U=-H^*F(\partial_s,\partial_t)U$. Here [F3] identifies the pulled-back two-form as the curvature of the supplier connection. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Since $\operatorname{rank}(dH)\le1$ on $\Delta$, $H_s,H_t$ are linearly dependent and the alternating two-form satisfies $H^*F(\partial_s,\partial_t)=F(H_s,H_t)=0$. Fix a vertex $q_0$ and join it to each $q\in\Delta$ by the image of the straight radial path in the standard-simplex parametrization. The associated transports $Q(q)$ exist globally by [F5] and depend smoothly on $q$: apply [F4] locally in the endpoint parameter and continue over finitely many subintervals of the compact path interval, using uniqueness on overlaps. For each radial path, [F3] and the ODE give $(Q^{\mathsf T}\eta Q)'=0$, hence $Q(q)^{\mathsf T}\eta Q(q)=\eta$ and $Q(q)$ is invertible. Step 1.1 on this radial family with fixed start gives $dQ=-H^*\omega\,Q$. Thus transport from $q_1$ to $q_2$ in $\Delta$ is $Q(q_2)Q(q_1)^{-1}$ by [F5], and the triangle boundary transport is identity. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The finite curvilinear-triangle subdivision is a finite connected CW complex $K$; choose the lower-left corner as basepoint and a maximal tree in its one-skeleton. The outer boundary loop contracts to that basepoint by the straight-line contraction of the parameter square, so [F6] makes its fundamental-group class the identity. By [F7], $\pi_1(K)$ has generators given by non-tree edge loops closed along the tree and relators given by based triangular face boundaries.
